title: Contextual Sparsity & KV-cache Strategies — reading + experiment notes
content:
Quick overview:
This is a personal scratchpad summarizing recent papers/blogs about contextual sparsity, KV-cache compression, and routing heuristics for long-context inference. Collecting ideas to try on Redwood: microbenchmarks + cheap evals that reflect production prompt mixes. Not polished — mostly notes, hypotheses, and action items.

Key takeaways from readings:
- Contextual sparsity (pruning/soft-attention sparsity) looks promising for reducing KV size for very long contexts without linear blowup in latency. Papers use top-k / locality masks and learned gating. Tradeoff: token-level recall vs end-task accuracy.
- KV-cache compression via product quantization / residual quantization often recovers most retrieval quality with <=8x memory reduction, but decode latency increases slightly for lookups if naive. Need fast C bindings or GPU kernels for PQ lookup.
- Adaptive eviction policies (age+salience scoring) beat pure LRU for multi-session workloads where prefix reuse is common. Salience can be estimated via attention-weight backfills or simple recency-frequency heuristics.
- MoE and routing: cheap routing decisions (hashed or locality sensitive) can reduce compute but introduce staleness in cached keys; must consider consistency when using layered fallbacks.

Notes to self (practical for Redwood):
- Build a tiny benchmark harness that replays real logged prefix lengths from hosted API (sample by customer tier). Measure: end-to-end p50/p95 latency, token-cost delta, and downstream task surprisals.
- Implement a baseline "KV-PQ" prototype: CPU-side PQ for KV vectors + a cached lookup table on GPU for hot clusters. Evaluate memory reduction and lookup time for sequence lengths 4k/8k/16k.
- Try 3 eviction policies: LRU, LRU+salience (attention mass), and scored-age with decay factor. Use synthetic workload that mixes short chat sessions and long-document sessions.
- Quick experiment matrix: quant bits = [8,6,4], PQ centroids = [64,128], eviction windows = [1k,4k,16k tokens]. Capture failure modes (hallucination increase, concat-bleed).

Unresolved questions / risks:
- How to measure "quality loss" cheaply? Best proxy: masked-perplexity on held-out prompt continuation sets + a small classification/regression downstream probe. Need to pick 2–3 prod-like tasks (summarization, QA, code-gen).
- Operational complexity: PQ tables + staged lookup adds engineering surface. Is the unit-cost win worth the extra failure modes for hosted customers? Possibly for Dedicated/Private where memory is a bottleneck.
- Security: compressed vectors might change leakage profile; discuss with security/compliance before enabling on private deployments.

Short reference notes (papers/blogs skimmed):
- "Sparse Attention for Long Sequences" — shows tradeoffs on recall vs sparsity density. Implementation notes: top-k attention with block-sparse kernels works well on GPUs for chunked queries.
- "Product Quantization for Neural Representations" — good baseline math and PQ hyperparams.
- Blog: "KV-cache at scale" — practical pitfalls (eviction storms, cold-start cost).

Actionables (next 3 weeks):
- [ ] Get sample replay logs from infra (ask Diego for a small extract of 10k requests by prefix length distribution).
- [ ] Prototype PQ-backed KV lookup (Python+numpy prototype to validate compression ratios). Owner: Quinn.
- [ ] Run quick end-to-end bench on local 80GB A100 (4k,8k,16k) and collect perf/quality deltas. Owner: Ava.
- [ ] Sync with Security (short note) about information leakage concerns.

Quick heuristics brainstorm (one-liners):
- If prefix reuse rate > 30% for a model + route, favor keeping uncompressed cold keys (hot-cold split).
- Use approximate attention backprop (salience by forward-pass attention mass) as a cheap salience signal for eviction.
- Fall back to smaller quantized cache when latency SLOs tight; fall back to full cache during canary if regression detected.

Random notes to capture: 
- Consider PV-tree style quant search for faster PQ lookups (GPU-friendly).
- Might combine with dynamic batching: compress cold keys offline and decompress small working set on-demand.

End — this is a living doc. Keep sketching experiments and move promising items into a proper RFC if bench results look good.
